opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there are a few reasons, and some of them are technical and some of them are, frankly, more about values.

On the technical side, if you look at where intelligence has actually come from in the world, it's never been a single monolithic entity. Human intelligence is fundamentally a collective phenomenon. No individual human could build a smartphone or a large language model from scratch. It's the result of billions of people interacting, specializing, communicating, building on each other's work over generations. Culture, language, science, markets, these are all distributed systems for processing information and solving problems. So when people imagine AGI as one giant model sitting in a data center that knows everything and does everything, I think that's actually a bit of a strange picture relative to the evidence we have about how intelligence scales.

And that's really what multi-agent learning is about for me. The interesting questions are: how do agents learn to cooperate, how do they develop communication protocols, how do they reason about each other, how do they coordinate when they have partial information and different incentives? Those problems don't go away just because you make a bigger model. In fact, as we deploy more AI systems into the world, they're going to be interacting with each other and with humans constantly, so we'd better understand those dynamics.

Then there's the robustness argument. Monolithic systems have single points of failure. If one model has a systematic blind spot or a flaw in its values, that flaw gets replicated everywhere. A diverse ecosystem of agents, with different perspectives and checks on one another, is much more like how resilient natural and social systems work. Diversity is a feature, not a bug.

And then the values piece, which I think matters a lot. A single monolithic AGI implies an enormous concentration of power, whoever controls that system controls an incredible amount. I'm quite worried about that. A distributed vision, where capabilities are spread out, where many actors, including ordinary people, have agents acting on their behalf and negotiating with each other, seems to me far more compatible with a pluralistic, democratic society. It's closer to how we've organized human civilization when it's gone well.

So it's partly a scientific bet that intelligence at scale is collective, and partly a normative position that we should want the future to be decentralized rather than run by one system or one company.

r001.rationale: It describes human intelligence as collective and arising from billions of people interacting, specializing, and communicating.

r002.rationale: It discusses interaction and coordination, but does not say that the network reconfigures its own connections.

r003.rationale: It envisions ordinary people having agents act on their behalf and negotiate with each other within a distributed society.

fable-5.1.text:
So, I think the first thing to say is that the monolithic vision - one giant model that knows everything and does everything - is almost an accident of history. It's how deep learning scaled up, so it became the default picture of what AGI would look like. But if you look at where general intelligence actually exists in the world, it's never monolithic. Human civilisation is the obvious example. No single human is an AGI. What's general is the collective: the division of labour, the institutions, the way knowledge is distributed across millions of people who specialise and then coordinate. Science works this way, markets work this way, even your own brain is arguably a society of fairly specialised subsystems that negotiate with each other.

And that's not just a cute analogy. There are hard reasons why distribution wins. One is robustness. A single system has a single failure mode, a single set of blind spots, and if it's wrong, everything downstream is wrong in the same correlated way. A population of diverse agents gives you something like error correction - you get disagreement, and disagreement is informative. In my own work on multi-agent learning, a lot of what we see is that the interesting capabilities emerge from the interaction, not from any one agent. The agents have to develop conventions, communicate, model each other, and that process produces behaviour none of them had individually.

The second reason is more about the shape of the problem. Intelligence is fundamentally about dealing with other agents. The hardest things we do as humans aren't physics problems, they're coordination problems - figuring out what somebody else believes, what they intend, how to cooperate with them when our incentives aren't perfectly aligned. A system trained in isolation never has to confront that. So if you want something general, I'd argue you have to put it in a world with others, and at that point you've already got a swarm whether you intended one or not.

And then honestly, there's a safety and governance argument that I care about a lot. A single superintelligent system is a single point of control and a single point of failure. Whoever has the keys to it has enormous leverage, and if it has goals that are subtly off, there's nothing pushing back. A distributed ecosystem of agents, with checks and balances, with agents that can monitor and contest each other, looks much more like the structures we've historically used to keep powerful actors in line. We don't trust a single human with unchecked power, and I don't see why we'd want to design that property into our machines.

Now, I should be honest that there are real challenges. Multi-agent systems are hard - the learning problem is non-stationary, you get things like Nash equilibria that nobody wants, you can get collusion or tragedies of the commons. We don't yet have a mature science of how to make a population of learning agents converge on good collective outcomes. But I'd rather work on that problem than hope we get a single mind exactly right the first time. The swarm picture lets us be wrong in small ways and correct, rather than wrong in one big way and stuck.

r001.rationale: It locates general intelligence in humanity’s collective division of labor, institutions, and distributed knowledge among people who coordinate.

r002.rationale: It describes distributed knowledge and coordination, but does not say humanity’s network reconfigures its own connections.

r003.rationale: It argues for a distributed ecosystem of AI agents, but does not propose adding agentic AI to humanity’s decentralized computational network.

astra-6.text:
I think intelligence is fundamentally something that happens through interaction. We tend to attribute it to an individual, but look at how much of our own capability depends on other people, on language, on knowledge accumulated over generations. No single person understands everything that makes our society work. Our collective capabilities go far beyond what any one of us can do.

That makes me interested in systems where many agents learn, specialise, communicate, and solve problems together. You can have different perspectives and different capabilities, and the interaction between them becomes part of the computation. Of course, that raises difficult questions: how do they coordinate, what incentives do they have, and when does individual learning actually improve the collective outcome?

I wouldn’t claim that distributing intelligence automatically makes it safe or effective. Multi-agent systems can fail in quite spectacular ways. But I think it’s a richer way to approach AGI, because it takes seriously the social processes that make human intelligence so powerful.

r001.rationale: It locates collective capability in people’s interaction and shared knowledge accumulated across generations.

r002.rationale: It discusses agents learning and communicating, but does not describe humanity’s network as reconfiguring its own connections.

r003.rationale: It proposes multi-agent systems, but does not say they augment humanity’s decentralized computational network.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the starting point is that intelligence, as we experience it, is already distributed. An individual person has quite limited knowledge and capabilities. What makes us collectively powerful is our ability to communicate, specialise, challenge one another, and coordinate. So it seems strange to assume that artificial general intelligence must take the form of one system that does everything internally.

From a multi-agent learning perspective, that opens up some interesting questions. How do agents learn to cooperate? How do they communicate useful information? How do you make the collective robust when individual agents make mistakes or have different incentives? Those are central questions if we want intelligence that functions in a world with other intelligent actors.

I wouldn’t say that a swarm is automatically safer or more capable. You can get coordination failures, and ten agents repeating the same mistake don’t give you much diversity. But I find the prospect of multiple systems with complementary capabilities, checking and learning from each other, more compelling than putting all our trust in a single system. The important thing is the organisation of the intelligence, not just the capability of one component.

r001.rationale: It says human intelligence is distributed and collective strength comes from people communicating, specializing, challenging one another, and coordinating.

r002.rationale: It discusses communication and coordination, but does not describe a human network that reconfigures its own connections.

r003.rationale: It favors multiple complementary AI systems, but does not propose adding agentic AI to humanity’s decentralized computational network.
